plain: Higgsfield is a website where you describe a video shot in words and it generates it for you: you can start from a photo of yourself and have the camera pull back, have the subject turn, get a tracking shot or an overhead shot. What sets it apart from other AI video tools is that you don't leave the camera movement to chance: you pick the movement from a list, the way you'd choose a shot on a film set. It's good for short ads, product videos, social content, and five-to-ten-second pieces that you later edit together. The honest comparison: it's not a production studio, it's a very fast camera that sometimes gets it wrong and doesn't understand what your brand is about.

account.free: You work with credits, not time: each video generation uses up an amount that depends on the model and the length. There's a free plan for trying it out, with a watermark and a queue when it's busy. Paid plans started around $9 a month for the basic tier and went up quite a bit for plans meant for daily production, as of August 2026. Check for yourself at higgsfield.ai: in this category, prices and plan names change every few months. Two warnings that matter more than the price: check whether your plan allows commercial use before putting a video into a client's ad, and check whether it removes the watermark, because the free plan doesn't.
steps: Type it into your browser's address bar. As with every trending tool, there are imitations advertised on search engines and social media; the real site is higgsfield.ai.

That's the fastest way. You'll land on a dashboard with examples of videos generated by other people: pay attention to them, because underneath each one there's usually the prompt used to make it, and it's the best way to learn what you can ask for.
Check your credits before generating anything

Find the counter in your profile. Note how many you have and how much a generation costs with the model you're going to use. A five-second video can cost as much as twenty images: better to know that before than after.
Check two things about your plan before using it for a client
One: whether it allows commercial use. Two: whether it removes the watermark. They're on the plans page and in the terms. If you're going to bill for a video made here, this isn't a minor detail.
Make your first generation with a photo of your own, not text

Start from a photo: a product photo, a portrait, a shot of your storefront. Results starting from an image are much more predictable than ones from a description alone, and you learn faster how the tool responds.
Choose the camera movement from the list

This is the step that makes this tool special and the one people skip. Before writing the description, choose whether you want a slow zoom, a turn around the subject, an overhead shot, or a tracking shot. The movement changes the result more than any adjectives you add.
account.warning: Never upload someone's face without their explicit permission, and even less so a well-known person's. Generating video with someone else's face has real legal consequences, it's not a prank, and a person's image is legally protected. The same rule applies to customer data: a product shot, yes; a video of an identifiable person that came in over WhatsApp, no.

first: Look at ten examples on the home dashboard and read the prompt underneath each one. You'll learn more in five minutes than reading the documentation.
Upload a photo of your product or storefront and generate a single short shot with a smooth camera movement from the list.
Check the result for the usual flaws: hands, written text, logos, and eyes. That's almost always where it breaks.
Repeat the same prompt changing ONE thing only: the camera movement. Compare the two. That's how you understand what really drives the result.
Write down in a file the prompt that worked best, along with the model and movement used. Without that notebook, you won't be able to repeat a win.
shortcuts: The camera movement list

The heart of the tool. Zoom in, zoom out, orbit around the subject, side tracking shot, overhead, low angle. Choosing from the list works much better than describing the movement in words in the text.
Image to video
You start from a photo of your own and set it in motion. It's the mode to start with: results are much more predictable than text-to-video, because the starting point is already fixed.
Text to video
Only a description. It gives you more surprises and more rejects. Use it when you have no material of your own or when you're after something abstract.
Shot length
Almost always between five and ten seconds. Don't think 'a video': think shots you'll edit together later. Asking for one long video in one go is the classic beginner mistake.
The seed
A number that fixes the randomness. With the same seed, the same prompt, and the same settings, the result comes out similar. It's what lets you repeat a win instead of just hoping.
The model selector

There are several generation engines, and they don't cost the same or serve the same purpose. Before spending twenty credits, generate a short test with the cheap one to see if the shot's framing works.
The generation queue
Your video doesn't come out instantly: it enters a queue. At peak times it can take a while. Don't click generate again thinking it didn't register: you'll spend double the credits.
The gallery or history
Everything you've generated, with its prompt next to it. It's your archive and your working notebook: this is where you retrieve the prompts that worked.
Downloading at maximum quality
Always download at the best quality your plan gives you, even if you're going to post it on social media. Regenerating because you saved a small version costs credits all over again.
The watermark
On the free plan it's added and can't be removed by editing. If the video is for a client, this is solved with the plan, not with cropping.
daily: Think in shots, not videos. Everything that comes out well here is a five-to-ten-second piece. A thirty-second video gets edited together afterward from four or five shots; it isn't requested in one go.
Always start from a photo of your own. A product photo, your storefront, or a real object anchors the result and saves you half the rejects. Pure text is for when you don't have any material.
Change only one thing between attempts. If you change the movement, the model, and the description all at once, you won't know what improved the result, and you'll be spending credits blind.

Always check hands, text, logos, and eyes. Those are the four places where AI video breaks down, and they're exactly where the human eye looks first. A gorgeous shot with a six-fingered hand is unusable.
Keep a notebook of prompts that worked, with the model, the movement, and the seed. Without that, every win is unrepeatable and you're starting from zero every morning.
Check commercial use before billing. If the video is going into a client's ad, your plan needs to allow it and the watermark needs to be gone. Check this before accepting the job, not after.

Count credits the way you count money. Before a long session, check how many you have and decide how many attempts you'll allow yourself per shot. Without that cap, one afternoon eats up the whole month.

templates.name: The shot sheet: what to fill in before generating
templates.what: Generating without deciding first is how people burn through credits. This sheet takes two minutes to fill in per shot and forces you to make the four decisions that actually change the result: what's shown, how the camera moves, what light there is, and how long it lasts. It works equally well for an ad, a product video, or a social piece.
templates.how: 1) Fill in one sheet per shot, not one for the whole video. 2) Be specific about the subject: 'white sneaker on wet concrete' works; 'modern product' doesn't. 3) Choose the movement from the tool's list, don't describe it with adjectives. 4) Generate. 5) Write down the seed and model next to it if you like the result.
fill: Exactly what's shown. A specific object, not a category
Chosen from the tool's list. It's what changes the result the most
Time of day and hardness. Changes the tone more than any adjective
Between 5 and 10 seconds. Long shots come out badly
Write it down when something works: it's how you repeat a win
templates.code:
SHOT SHEET  ·  [PROJECT NAME]  ·  shot [1 of 5]

STARTING FROM:  [ ] a photo of mine   [ ] text only
FILE:            [photo-name.jpg]

SUBJECT:         [WHAT'S SHOWN, SPECIFIC]
                 e.g.: white sneaker on wet concrete

SETTING:         [WHERE IT IS]
                 e.g.: city street at dawn, no people

MOVEMENT:        [CHOSEN FROM THE LIST]
                 e.g.: slow orbit around the subject

LIGHT:           [TIME AND HARDNESS]
                 e.g.: early morning, soft side light, long shadows

LENGTH:          [5 / 8 / 10 seconds]
MODEL:           [WHICH]
ESTIMATED COST:  [CREDITS]

--- after generating ---
SEED:            [WRITE IT DOWN IF IT WORKED]
USABLE:          [ ] yes   [ ] no, because [HANDS / TEXT / LOGO / EYES]

RULE: maximum [3] attempts per shot. If it's still not right on the third,
I change the whole prompt, not just one adjective.

templates.name: The script for a 20-second ad, shot by shot
templates.what: This is the structure used in short-form advertising, and it works on social media: hook them in the first second, show the problem, show the solution, and close with what you want people to do. Each box is a five-second shot you generate separately and then put together in any editor.
templates.how: 1) Fill in the four boxes before generating anything. 2) Generate the four shots separately, each with its own sheet. 3) Put them together in the script's order in any free editor. 4) Music and on-screen text go in during editing, not requested from the AI. 5) Watch it on your phone with no sound: that's how 80% of people will see it.
fill: The first second decides whether they keep watching. Fast movement or something odd
The uncomfortable situation your customer recognizes as their own
Your product doing what it does. This is the shot to put the most care into
Brand and what to do now. The text is added during editing
templates.code:
20-SECOND AD  ·  [PRODUCT]
For: [WHO WILL SEE IT]   ·   Where: [INSTAGRAM / TIKTOK / WEBSITE]
Format: [vertical 9:16 / horizontal 16:9]

─ SHOT 1 · HOOK (0-5 s) ───────────────────────────────────
Shown:        [WHAT]
Movement:     [fast zoom in / sharp turn]
Why it stops the scroll: [WHAT'S ODD OR EYE-CATCHING ABOUT IT]

─ SHOT 2 · PROBLEM (5-10 s) ───────────────────────────────
Shown:        [THE UNCOMFORTABLE SITUATION]
Movement:     [slow tracking shot / static camera]

─ SHOT 3 · SOLUTION (10-15 s) ─────────────────────────────
Shown:        [YOUR PRODUCT IN USE]
Movement:     [slow orbit / gentle zoom in]
Note:         this is the shot worth spending the most attempts on

─ SHOT 4 · CLOSE (15-20 s) ────────────────────────────────
Shown:        [PRODUCT IN A CLEAN SHOT, NEUTRAL BACKGROUND]
Movement:     [slow zoom out]
Text overlay: [ADDED DURING EDITING, NOT REQUESTED FROM THE AI]

─ CHECKS BEFORE DELIVERING ─────────────────────────────────
[ ] Watched on the phone, no sound, all the way through
[ ] Hands, text, logos, and eyes checked across all 4 shots
[ ] No watermark
[ ] My plan allows commercial use
[ ] No identifiable person appears without having given permission

errors: The video comes out with deformed hands or extra fingers

It's the classic video-generation flaw and doesn't get fixed by insisting with the same prompt. Three ways out, in order: frame the shot so the hands don't appear (tighter or wider shot), have the subject hold something so the hands are occupied, or switch to a shot with no people. A gorgeous shot with a bad hand is an unusable shot: the eye goes straight there.
The text that appears in the video is misspelled or unreadable

AI video doesn't know how to write: it draws something that looks like letters. Don't waste credits trying to get your brand name spelled correctly. Generate the shot without text and add the text on top during editing, with any editor. That's what's actually done in real production, not a workaround.
My brand's logo comes out distorted

Same problem as the text. Same solution: generate the shot without the logo and overlay it afterward during editing, where it'll also be sharp and the exact right size. Asking the AI to respect a specific logo is throwing away credits.
It's stuck in the queue and not moving

At peak times generations take longer, and on the free plan you're behind paying users. The costly mistake is clicking generate again thinking it didn't register: two get queued and you pay for two. Wait, check the history before repeating, and if you're going to produce daily, factor the queue into your planning.

They've run out. There's no shortcut: either wait for the cycle to reset or upgrade your plan. What you can do is stop it from happening mid-job: before starting, divide the credits you have among the shots you need and set a maximum number of attempts per shot. Without that cap, the first shot eats up half the month.
The result doesn't look anything like what I asked for

It's almost always that the prompt was a list of adjectives ('modern, elegant, striking') instead of a description of what's shown. Rewrite it stating the specific subject, the specific setting, the light, and the movement, and choose the movement from the list instead of describing it. And if you started from text only, try starting from a photo: the quality jump is huge.
Every attempt comes out different and I can't repeat the one I liked

You're not locking the seed. That number is what makes the randomness the same. When something works, write down the seed, model, movement, and prompt in your notebook; without that, a win can't be reproduced or tweaked slightly, which is exactly what you're going to want to do.
The video has a watermark and the client has seen it

The free plan adds it, and it can't be removed by cropping or editing: it's part of the image. Solved by upgrading the plan before generating the final version. And while you're at it, check the other thing people forget: that your plan allows commercial use if you're going to bill for that video.

prompts.name: Turn an ad idea into generatable shots
prompts.prompt: Act as an art director who works with AI-generated video and knows its limits. I'm going to tell you the ad I have in mind, and I want you to turn it into shots that Higgsfield can actually generate, not a pretty idea that won't come out right later. Do it like this. One: ask me at most four questions about the product, who's going to see it, where it'll be published, and what I want that person to do after watching it. Two: break the ad into four or five five-second shots, and for each one tell me exactly what's shown, in what setting, with what light, and with what camera movement, choosing the movement from the ones that exist in the tool (zoom in, zoom out, orbit, tracking shot, overhead, low angle). Three: for each shot, tell me whether it's better to start from a photo of mine or generate it from text only, and why. Four: warn me which of the shots I've asked for are a bad idea because they include close-up hands, written text, logos, or recognizable faces, and suggest another way to achieve the same thing. Five: tell me which shot is worth spending more attempts on and for which ones the first decent result is fine. Six: tell me what needs to happen in later editing rather than in generation: text, music, logo, subtitles. My ad is for: [PRODUCT] and the idea I have is: [DESCRIBE IT].

prompts.name: Write the exact prompt for a specific shot
prompts.prompt: I need the exact text to generate a video shot in Higgsfield, and I want you to write it for me, because when I write it myself I end up with adjectives instead of descriptions. I'll give you what I'm trying to achieve, and you give me back the prompt ready to paste. Before writing it, tell me in two lines what you understood the shot to show, so I can correct you before spending credits. Then give me: one, the prompt in a single paragraph, written to describe what's shown rather than what I want to convey, with the specific subject, the specific setting, the time of day, and the hardness of the light; two, which camera movement from the list to choose and why that one; three, what length to request; four, three variants of the same prompt, each changing ONE thing only, so I can compare without getting confused; five, what's likely to go wrong in this specific shot and what I should check for when reviewing it; six, if my idea is one of the kind that works better starting from a photo, tell me what photo I'd need to take and how. The shot I need is: [DESCRIBE IT AS BEST YOU CAN, EVEN IF ROUGHLY]. It's for: [WHERE IT WILL BE SEEN].

prompts.name: Diagnose why my videos are coming out wrong
prompts.prompt: I've made several attempts in Higgsfield and the results don't look like what I want. I'm going to paste the prompts I've used and what came out. I want an honest diagnosis, not encouragement. Answer me like this. One: tell me what my prompts have in common that's causing this, pointing to specific phrases of mine; be harsh if needed. Two: tell me which of my problems are due to how I'm writing and which are limits of the technology that I won't be able to solve no matter how much I insist, so I stop spending credits on the latter. Three: rewrite one of my prompts, whichever you think is most salvageable, and explain line by line what you changed and why. Four: tell me which settings I'm ignoring (camera movement, model, length, seed, starting from an image) that would change the result more than continuing to polish the text. Five: tell me how many attempts is reasonable to spend on a shot before accepting that the shot needs to be rethought entirely. Six: if what I'm trying to achieve simply can't be done today with this tool, tell me clearly and tell me what it can be done with. My prompts have been: [PASTE THEM]. What came out: [DESCRIBE IT].

prompts.name: Check whether I can use this for a client
prompts.prompt: I'm going to bill a client for a video made with AI, and I want to be clear on what could come back to bite me. Don't give me generic legal boilerplate: ask me whatever questions you need about my specific case, then tell me what I'm exposed to and what I need to check. Cover these points for me. One: exactly what I need to look at in my plan to know whether commercial use is allowed, and where it's written. Two: who owns what I generate, what rights I have over it, and what happens if the client wants exclusivity. Three: what's the risk that the result looks too much like an existing work or someone's recognizable style, and how I reduce that. Four: what rules exist about disclosing that content is AI-generated in advertising, both in the US and in the EU, and what happens if I don't disclose it. Five: what I should never do, especially with real people's faces, with minors, and with brands that aren't mine. Six: what I need to put in writing for the client in the quote to cover myself, in two or three sentences I can copy. And if at any point the right answer is to consult a lawyer, tell me that instead of improvising. My case: [WHAT VIDEO, FOR WHICH CLIENT, WHERE IT WILL BE PUBLISHED].

prompts.name: Plan the credits for a full delivery
prompts.prompt: I have to deliver [WHAT: a 20-second ad / five product videos / a campaign] and I want to know whether the credits I have will be enough before I accept the job. Help me do the math and organize the session. One: ask me how many credits I have, what plan it is, and how much each generation costs with the model I plan to use. Two: tell me how many distinct shots what I need to deliver actually requires, and whether any can be reused or trimmed in editing instead of generated separately. Three: give me an attempts-per-shot budget, being realistic about the first ones coming out wrong, and tell me which shot is the one to concentrate the spending on. Four: tell me what order to generate in, starting with the shot most at risk of not working, so if it doesn't I find out on day one and not on the last day. Five: tell me what I can do in editing to save on generations: reversing a shot, freezing a frame, extending with a transition. Six: tell me how much margin to leave for client changes, because there always are some. And if what I have isn't enough, tell me so with the number in front of me so I can upgrade my plan or adjust the budget before committing.

words: Credit
The tool's currency. Each generation uses up a certain amount depending on the model and length. Plan them ahead of time, like money.
Image to video
Starting from a photo of your own and setting it in motion. It's the most predictable mode and the one to start with.
Text to video
Generating from a description alone. Freer, but with many more rejects.
Camera movement
How the point of view moves: zooming in, zooming out, orbiting, moving sideways, looking down from above. Chosen from a list, and it's what changes the result the most.
Shot
A continuous piece of video, five to ten seconds long. You work in shots here, and the video gets edited together afterward.
Seed
A number that fixes the randomness. With the same seed and the same prompt, the result comes out similar. It's how you repeat a win.
Model
The engine that generates. There are several, they don't cost the same, and they don't serve the same purpose. Try the cheap one before reaching for the expensive one.
Queue
The generation waiting list. At peak times it takes longer. Repeating out of impatience doubles the spend.
Watermark
The mark the free plan embeds in the video. It doesn't come off by cropping: it comes off with the plan.
Commercial use
Whether your plan lets you use what's generated in something you charge for. Check this BEFORE accepting a client job.
matters: Think in five-to-ten-second shots and edit them together afterward. Everything that comes out well here is short pieces. Asking for one long video in a single go is the fastest way to burn credits on something unusable.

Choose the camera movement from the list instead of describing it with adjectives. It's what sets this tool apart from the others, and it's what changes the result the most. People ignore it and then complain everything comes out flat.

Check commercial use and the watermark before accepting a client job. Finding out your plan doesn't allow billing with that after you've already delivered is a serious and perfectly avoidable problem.
Write down the seed, model, and prompt for everything that comes out well. Without that notebook, every win is unrepeatable and you start from zero every morning.
ignore: Having the AI write text or draw your logo inside the video. It doesn't know how, and it won't learn no matter how much you insist. That goes on top during editing, where it'll also come out sharp and whatever size you want.
The advanced model settings while you're still learning. Changing three parameters at once means you can't tell what improved the result. The defaults are fine for your first fifty generations.
Chasing absolute realism in shots with people. That's where the technology still breaks down. Shots of products, objects, environments, and details come out much better and are the ones that sell.
